title: Paediatric Hip and Knee Conditions: DDH, Perthes Disease, SCFE and Osgood-Schlatter

rows: Shallow or unstable hip socket; hip may dislocate
Temporary hip inflammation after a viral illness; resolves
Loss of blood supply to the femoral head; bone softens and remodels
About 10 to 16 years, often overweight, growth spurt
Femoral head slips off the neck at the growth plate
Traction irritation at the tibial tuberosity growth plate
Traction irritation of the heel growth plate (Achilles insertion)

items: **Limping child** is the key presentation for hip conditions.
SCFE and Perthes often present with **knee or thigh pain**, not hip pain. Always examine the hip in a child with knee pain.
Osgood-Schlatter: pain and swelling at the tibial tuberosity with running, jumping, kneeling.

blocks.label: MEMORY HOOK
body: "Knee pain in a child: examine the hip." Hip pain is often referred to the knee via the obturator nerve.

blocks.text: Age; onset (sudden or gradual); trauma; fever, unwell; ability to bear weight; pain at night; recent viral illness; growth spurt; sports load; family history (DDH).

sections.title: D to E. Examination and tests

rows: Barlow and Ortolani tests (newborn screening by trained staff)
Barlow: hip can be pushed out; Ortolani: dislocated hip "clunks" back in
Knee heights unequal in crook lying
Obligatory external rotation with hip flexion
The thigh rolls into external rotation as you flex the hip
Very painful, held flexed, any movement painful
Medical assessment to exclude septic arthritis

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Fever, unwell, refusing to bear weight, severe pain on any hip movement
Adolescent with hip, thigh or knee pain and obligatory external rotation; unable to bear weight
Night pain, weight loss, bruising, pallor

steps: **Limping child: fever or unable to bear weight?** Emergency.
**Adolescent with reduced internal rotation and obligatory ER?** Suspected SCFE: stop weight-bearing; urgent orthopaedics.
**Young child, gradual limp, reduced IR?** Perthes: orthopaedic referral.
**Active adolescent with tuberosity pain, normal hip?** Osgood-Schlatter: load management.

items: **DDH**: managed by orthopaedics (harness, casting, surgery); physiotherapy for range and gross motor development after treatment.
**Perthes**: maintain hip range (especially abduction and internal rotation), strength, low-impact activity (swimming, cycling), activity modification as advised by orthopaedics.

**SCFE**: surgical fixation; physiotherapy after surgery for gait, strength and gradual return to sport per surgeon. **Osgood-Schlatter and Sever disease**: education (self-limiting, settles with growth plate closure); load management (reduce jumping volume, not complete rest); quadriceps or calf strengthening and flexibility; pain-guided return; heel raise insert for Sever. Pain up to about 3 to 4/10 during activity that settles by the next day is acceptable [Ref – to verify].
**Why examine the hip in a child with knee pain?** Hip conditions such as SCFE and Perthes often refer pain to the knee.
**What is obligatory external rotation?** The thigh rotates outward when the hip is flexed: a sign of SCFE.
**How do you separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis?** Fever, refusal to bear weight and a very unwell child suggest septic arthritis: emergency.
**Does Osgood-Schlatter need complete rest?** No. Load management and strengthening.
**Which age group typically gets Perthes?** About 4 to 8 years.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Recognise SCFE, Perthes, septic arthritis and DDH.
Manage growth-plate traction conditions with load management.
